fields.questionText:
A person allowed a narrow beam of white light from the sun to enter a dark room through a small aperture and placed a glass prism in its path so that the beam falls on the face AB of the prism. A screen S is placed on the other side of the prism, facing AC. On turning the prism slowly, a beautiful band of colours is obtained on the screen. It is the spectrum of sunlight.
(a) Name the phenomenon due to which a prism splits the incident white light into a band of colours. (1)
(b) State the reason for getting a band of seven colours in the above case. (1)
(c) (i) Explain with the help of a labelled ray diagram an experimental arrangement to show the recombination of the spectrum of white light. (2)
OR
(c) (ii) Draw a labelled ray diagram to show the formation of a rainbow. (2)
fields.answer: (a) Dispersion of light. (b) Different colours of light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through the prism. (c)(i) Two identical prisms are placed in inverted position with respect to each other; when the spectrum produced by prism A passes through prism B, a beam of white light emerges from prism B. OR (c)(ii) Labelled diagram: sunlight refracted and dispersed on entering a raindrop, internally reflected at the back, refracted again on leaving, red and violet emerging separately.
solutionSteps: (a) Dispersion of light.
(b) Different colours of white light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through a prism, so they separate into seven colours.
(c)(i) Diagram: two identical prisms A and B, with B placed inverted with respect to A; white light enters A, is dispersed into a spectrum which then falls on B.
(c)(i) The spectrum produced by prism A, on passing through prism B, recombines and a beam of white light emerges from the other side of prism B.
OR (c)(ii) Diagram: a raindrop with sunlight refracted and dispersed on entering, internally reflected at the back surface, and refracted again on emerging, with red and violet rays labelled.
fields.finalAnswer: (a) Dispersion. (b) Different colours bend through different angles in the prism. (c)(i) Two identical prisms, the second inverted, recombine the spectrum into white light. OR (c)(ii) Rainbow: refraction + dispersion, internal reflection, refraction in a raindrop.

fields.questionText: A light ray AB is incident normally on face PQ of an equilateral glass prism PQR and travels undeviated to strike face PR. What is the angle of incidence of the ray at face PR?
solutionSteps: The ray falls normally on face PQ, so its angle of incidence there is 0° and it passes undeviated, perpendicular to PQ. Since the angle between faces PQ and PR of an equilateral prism is 60°, the normal to PR makes 60° with the normal to PQ, so the angle of incidence at face PR is 60°. Hence option (a).

fields.questionText: Explain what causes long-sightedness (hypermetropia) and what can be done to correct it.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Cause: the focal length of the eye lens is too long (lens curvature is too small).
[1 mark] Cause: the eyeball has become too short, so the image of a near object forms behind the retina instead of on it.
[1 mark] Correction: use a convex (converging) lens of suitable power in spectacles or contact lenses (surgery is also possible) to bring the image onto the retina.

solutionSteps: [1 mark] Eye defects: short-sightedness (myopia), long-sightedness (hypermetropia), presbyopia and cataract.

[1 mark] Causes: change in shape/curvature of the eye lens, change in length of the eyeball, or change in position/flexibility of the lens; cataract is clouding of the lens (age, UV exposure, genetics).

fields.questionText:
Case Study: Rajesh, a 45-year-old man, visits an eye clinic complaining that he can see distant objects clearly but has difficulty reading newspapers. His daughter, who is 12 years old, complains that she cannot see the board at school clearly but can read books comfortably. Both require different types of lenses for correction.

(i) What is the vision defect of Rajesh, and what type of lens would he need? (1)
(ii) Identify the vision defect of Rajesh's daughter and suggest an appropriate lens type. (1)
(iii) Explain the role of the ciliary muscles in accommodation and why accommodation fails in Rajesh's case. (2)
fields.answer: (i) Rajesh has presbyopia; he needs a convex lens. (ii) The daughter has myopia; she needs a concave lens. (iii) Ciliary muscles change the curvature (and focal length) of the eye lens for accommodation. In presbyopia, ageing weakens the ciliary muscles and reduces the flexibility of the eye lens, so the lens cannot become thick enough for near vision.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) He sees far objects clearly but not near ones at age 45 → presbyopia; corrected with a convex lens.
[1 mark] (ii) She cannot see distant objects but reads comfortably → myopia; corrected with a concave (diverging) lens.
[1 mark] (iii) Ciliary muscles contract or relax to change the curvature and focal length of the eye lens; for near objects they contract, making the lens thicker (more convex).
[1 mark] (iii) In presbyopia, ageing gradually weakens the ciliary muscles and reduces the flexibility of the eye lens, so the near point recedes and near objects cannot be focused.
fields.finalAnswer: (i) Presbyopia, convex lens. (ii) Myopia, concave lens. (iii) Ciliary muscles change lens curvature/focal length; in presbyopia weakened muscles and a less flexible lens prevent accommodation for near vision.

fields.questionText:
When white light is incident on one of the refracting surfaces of a prism, the light diverges into its constituent colours violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. This splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours is called dispersion, and the band of colours obtained on a screen is the spectrum. Red colour bends the least and violet bends the most on passing through the prism.
Answer the following questions:
a. What will happen when a red-coloured light is passed through a prism? (1)
b. Which type of spectrum is produced by white light when it is passed through a glass prism? (1)
c. Why does red light bend the least while violet light bends the most during dispersion? (2)
[OR]
c. Explain the cause of dispersion of white light through a prism. (2)

fields.questionText:
(A) Define the term dispersion of white light. State the colour which bends (i) the most, (ii) the least while passing through a glass prism. Draw a diagram to show the dispersion of white light.
OR
(B) What is a rainbow? Draw a labelled diagram to show its formation.
fields.answer: (A) Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours on passing through a glass prism. (i) Violet bends the most; (ii) red bends the least. Diagram: white light through a prism forming a spectrum with red at top (least deviated) and violet at bottom. OR (B) A rainbow is a natural spectrum of sunlight appearing in the sky after rainfall, formed by refraction, dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in tiny water droplets. Diagram: a raindrop refracting/dispersing sunlight, internally reflecting it and refracting it out, red and violet labelled.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (A) Dispersion: the splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours while passing through a glass prism.
[1 mark] (A) (i) Violet bends the most; (ii) red bends the least.
[1 mark] (A) Diagram: white light incident on a glass prism emerging as a band of colours, red (least deviated) at top and violet (most deviated) at bottom.
OR [1 mark] (B) A rainbow is a natural spectrum of sunlight appearing in the sky after rainfall, as tiny water droplets act like small prisms.

OR [2 marks] (B) Labelled diagram: sunlight entering a raindrop is refracted and dispersed, internally reflected at the back surface and refracted again on leaving; red and violet rays labelled, observer with Sun behind.
fields.finalAnswer: (A) Dispersion = splitting of white light into seven colours by a prism; violet bends most, red least. OR (B) Rainbow = natural spectrum of sunlight after rain, formed by refraction, dispersion and internal reflection in raindrops.
